pos: n. pl. (the linen screens of the tabernacle court; Hebrew qela')
etymology: From hang, Old English hangian, to suspend. The KJV keeps the plural for the curtains that were hung on pillars around the court, distinguishing them from the hanging (singular) that closed the gate.
biblical_def: The hangings are the wall of the tabernacle court — not a wall of stone or timber but of fine twined linen stretched between pillars set in sockets. The LORD commands, “And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side” (Exo 27:9). The north side matched it, “And likewise for the north side in length there shall be hangings of an hundred cubits long, and his twenty pillars and their twenty sockets of brass” (Exo 27:11), and the west side was shorter: “And for the breadth of the court on the west side shall be hangings of fifty cubits: their pillars ten, and their sockets ten” (Exo 27:12). When the work was done the record reads, “And he made the court: on the south side southward the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, an hundred cubits” (Exo 38:9). The hangings are the boundary of the holy. They are white, they are woven, they are man-high, and they say to Israel what a fence says: this far, and no farther, except by the gate. That a curtain rather than a rampart marked the line is itself instruction — the LORD guards His holiness by His word, not by masonry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hangings as linings for rooms; tapestry; drapery hung upon walls.
webster_full: HANGINGS, n. plu. Linings for rooms; tapestry; drapery hung upon walls.
HANG, v.t. To suspend; to fasten to some fixed object above, so that the thing is supported and swings freely.
2. To fit up or furnish with things suspended; as, to hang a room with tapestry.
scriptures: Exo 27:9
And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:

And likewise for the north side in length there shall be hangings of an hundred cubits long, and his twenty pillars and their twenty sockets of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets of silver.
And for the breadth of the court on the west side shall be hangings of fifty cubits: their pillars ten, and their sockets ten.
Exo 38:9
And he made the court: on the south side southward the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, an hundred cubits:
corruption_summary: A holy place with a linen boundary is read as a merely symbolic line, when Scripture treats it as a real one that cost a real death to cross wrongly.
corruption_paragraphs: The hangings were cloth, and cloth can be lifted. That is precisely why they instruct. The LORD did not need brass walls to keep Israel out; He needed only to say where the line was. Nadab and Abihu were consumed inside a tent, not inside a fortress. Modern readers who treat the court's linen as decoration have mistaken the softness of the material for softness in the command, and the whole tabernacle argues against them: the boundary is holy because the LORD drew it, not because it could not be breached.

The second thing the hangings settle is that access was never abolished, only located. There was one gate, and the gate had its own hanging of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen. A court fenced on all four sides with a single opening is a doctrine before it is a floor plan — and the Lord Jesus states it plainly when He says that He is the door. To keep the fence and lose the gate is legalism; to keep the gate and lose the fence is presumption. Exodus keeps both.
roots_summary: Hebrew qela' (H7050), a hanging or curtain of the court; from qala', to hang up; distinguished in the KJV from masak (H4539), the screen or hanging for a doorway.
roots_lines: Hebrew qela' (H7050) — the court hangings; Exodus 27:9, 27:11, 38:9.
Hebrew qala' (H7049) — to hang up, to sling; the verb behind the noun.
Hebrew masak (H4539) — a covering screen; rendered hanging (singular) for the gate and the door.
Hebrew shesh moshzar — fine twined linen; the material of the hangings throughout Exodus 27 and 38.
Hebrew chatser (H2691) — the court which the hangings enclose; Exodus 27:9.
usage: “There shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen” — a wall of cloth around a holy place.
“Their pillars ten, and their sockets ten” — the boundary is measured, not approximate.
The hangings fence the court; the gate opens it. Scripture keeps both.

pos: n. pl. (the blue fastenings of the tabernacle curtains; Hebrew lula'ah)
etymology: Middle English loupe, a noose or doubling of cord. The KJV uses it for the fifty blue eyes sewn along the selvedge of each curtain, into which the taches were set.
biblical_def: The loops are the small blue fastenings by which the tabernacle became one. “And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second” (Exo 26:4). Their number is exact: “Fifty loops shalt thou make in the one curtain, and fifty loops shalt thou make in the edge of the curtain that is in the coupling of the second; that the loops may take hold one of another” (Exo 26:5). Then the fastening: “And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one” (Exo 26:11). And it was done as commanded: “And he made loops of blue on the edge of one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling” (Exo 36:11). The purpose is stated in the text itself — that it may be one. Ten curtains and eleven curtains of goats' hair do not make a dwelling until the loops take hold one of another. The unity of the tabernacle was manufactured, counted, and commanded; it was not left to the fabric to find on its own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a loop as a folding or doubling of a string or rope, forming an opening through which another may be passed; a noose; a fastening.
webster_full: LOOP, n. A folding or doubling of a string or rope, or other flexible substance, through which a lace or cord may be passed for fastening.
2. An ornamental fold or doubling of ribbon or lace.
3. In fortification, a small narrow opening in the wall.
LOOPED, a. Bent or folded in the form of a loop; full of holes.
scriptures: Exo 26:4

And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second.
Exo 26:5
Fifty loops shalt thou make in the one curtain, and fifty loops shalt thou make in the edge of the curtain that is in the coupling of the second; that the loops may take hold one of another.
And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one.
And he made loops of blue on the edge of one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling: likewise he made in the uttermost side of another curtain, in the coupling of the second.
corruption_summary: Unity is treated as a mood the people generate, when Exodus makes it a fitting the LORD specified down to the count and the colour.
corruption_paragraphs: Fifty loops of blue, fifty taches, and the reason given in the same breath: that it may be one. The unity of the LORD's dwelling is engineered, and its engineering is commanded. This cuts against the modern instinct that unity is a feeling which arrives when a congregation is warm enough, and against the opposite error that unity is achieved by pruning away everyone who differs. Exodus offers a third thing: two distinct curtains, joined at a specified seam, by a specified fitting, in a specified number.

Note also the colour. The loops are blue — not the cheapest thread available, and not hidden work. The joints of the LORD's house were made of the same costly dye as the veil. That the fastenings were as carefully coloured as the coverings is a rebuke to every ministry that spends on what is seen and economizes on what holds the thing together.
roots_summary: Hebrew lula'ah (H3924), a loop or noose; used only of the tabernacle curtains; paired throughout with qeres (H7165), the tache or clasp that passed through it.
roots_lines: Hebrew lula'ah (H3924) — loop; Exodus 26:4, 26:5, 26:10, 36:11.
Hebrew qeres (H7165) — tache, clasp; the fitting inserted into the loop, Exodus 26:6, 26:11.
Hebrew tekeleth (H8504) — blue; the specified colour of every loop.
Hebrew chabar (H2266) — to couple, to join; the verb of the coupling the loops accomplish.
Hebrew echad (H259) — one; the stated purpose, that it may be one.
usage: “That the loops may take hold one of another” — the joint is the point.
“Couple the tent together, that it may be one” — unity as a commanded fitting.
Fifty loops of blue: the seams of the LORD's house were dyed like the veil.

pos: n. pl. (the vestibules or porches of Ezekiel's temple gates; Hebrew 'elam)
etymology: From Latin arcus, a bow. The KJV translators used arches for the porch-like recesses of the gateways in Ezekiel's vision, where later versions read porches or vestibules.
biblical_def: Arches belongs almost entirely to Ezekiel's temple vision, where the man with the measuring reed walks the prophet through gate after gate. “And there were narrow windows to the little chambers, and to their posts within the gate round about, and likewise to the arches: and windows were round about inward: and upon each post were palm trees” (Eze 40:16). The measurements repeat with deliberate monotony: “And the little chambers thereof were three on this side and three on that side; and the posts thereof and the arches thereof were after the measure of the first gate” (Eze 40:21), and again, “And their windows, and their arches, and their palm trees, were after the measure of the gate that looketh toward the east; and they went up unto it by seven steps; and the arches thereof were before them” (Eze 40:22). At the south gate the pattern holds: “And there were seven steps to go up to it, and the arches thereof were before them: and it had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, upon the posts thereof” (Eze 40:26). The arches are the threshold spaces — the place where a worshipper stands between the outside and the courts. Ezekiel is given no shortcut past them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an arch as a concave or curved structure supported by its own curve, and by extension the vault or portal so formed.
webster_full: ARCH, n. A segment or part of a circle; a concave or hollow structure of stone or brick, supported by its own curve.
2. The space between two piers; a vault.
3. A portal or entrance formed with a curved head.
ARCHED, a. Made with an arch or curve; covered with an arch.
scriptures: And there were narrow windows to the little chambers, and to their posts within the gate round about, and likewise to the arches: and windows were round about inward: and upon each post were palm trees.

And the little chambers thereof were three on this side and three on that side; and the posts thereof and the arches thereof were after the measure of the first gate: the length thereof was fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits.

And their windows, and their arches, and their palm trees, were after the measure of the gate that looketh toward the east; and they went up unto it by seven steps; and the arches thereof were before them.
And there were seven steps to go up to it, and the arches thereof were before them: and it had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, upon the posts thereof.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's measured gates are read as architectural filler to be skimmed, when the repetition is the prophet's point.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 40 is among the most skipped chapters in Scripture, and the arches are a large part of why: the same posts, the same windows, the same steps, gate after gate. But the tedium is the message. Israel had just lost a temple because worship had become improvised, and the vision answers with a building in which nothing is improvised. Every threshold is measured, and measured the same. A reader who finds the chapter dull has felt exactly what the exiles were meant to feel — the weight of a holiness that does not vary by gate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative one: the LORD does not merely accept worship, He specifies it. That a prophet in exile was given cubits rather than sentiments is a standing correction to every generation that would rather discuss worship than receive its pattern.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'elam (H361), a porch or vestibule of a gateway; concentrated in Ezekiel 40–41; the KJV renders it arches and, elsewhere, porch.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'elam (H361) — porch, arch; Ezekiel 40:16, 40:21, 40:22, 40:26.
Hebrew sha'ar (H8179) — gate; the structure the arches belong to.
Hebrew 'ayil (H352) — post, pilaster; paired with the arches in every measurement.
Hebrew timorah (H8561) — palm tree; the carved ornament upon the posts.
Hebrew qaneh (H7070) — the measuring reed in the hand of the man of brass.
usage: “The posts thereof and the arches thereof were after the measure of the first gate” — no gate is a special case.
“The arches thereof were before them” — a threshold you must cross, not a decoration.
Ezekiel 40 is measured, not described. The repetition is the doctrine.

pos: adj. (square; equal on all four sides; Hebrew rabua', Greek tetragonos)
etymology: Old English feower, four, and square, from Old French esquarre. The KJV keeps the compound where a thing is equal-sided by command, not merely rectangular.
biblical_def: Foursquare is the shape the LORD assigns to what is holy. The altar of burnt offering: “And thou shalt make an altar of shittim wood, five cubits long, and five cubits broad; the altar shall be foursquare” (Exo 27:1). The high priest's breastplate: “Foursquare it shall be being doubled; a span shall be the length thereof, and a span shall be the breadth thereof” (Exo 28:16). The altar of incense: “A cubit shall be the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof; foursquare shall it be” (Exo 30:2). And when the vision reaches its end, the same word carries the city: “And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal” (Rev 21:16). From the brazen altar in the wilderness to the New Jerusalem, the measure does not change. What God dwells in is equal on every side — no favoured face, no long side and short side, nothing that reads differently depending on where you stand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foursquare as having four sides and four angles equal; quadrangular.
webster_full: FOURSQUARE, a. Having four sides and four angles equal; quadrangular.
SQUARE, a. Having four equal sides and four right angles.
2. Just; exact; honest; fair; as square dealing.
scriptures: Exo 27:1
And thou shalt make an altar of shittim wood, five cubits long, and five cubits broad; the altar shall be foursquare: and the height thereof shall be three cubits.
Foursquare it shall be being doubled; a span shall be the length thereof, and a span shall be the breadth thereof.
Exo 30:2
A cubit shall be the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof; foursquare shall it be: and two cubits shall be the height thereof: the horns thereof shall be of the same.
And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal.
corruption_summary: Precise measurement in worship is dismissed as ancient pedantry, while Revelation ends the canon by measuring the city with a reed.
corruption_paragraphs: It is fashionable to treat the cubits of Exodus as cultural packaging around a timeless spiritual principle. Revelation 21 makes that reading impossible. The last vision of Scripture does not dissolve into abstraction; it takes a reed and measures. The city lieth foursquare. Whatever else the consummation is, it is not vaguer than the tabernacle — it is the same shape, larger.

The moral sense that English inherited from this word is not an accident. To call a man foursquare is to say he presents the same face on every side. Scripture's use runs the same direction: the altar, the breastplate over the priest's heart, and the city of God are all equal-sided, and the God who dwells among them is one in whom there is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
roots_summary: Hebrew rabua' (H7251), squared, four-sided; Greek tetragonos (G5068), four-cornered, used once, of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Hebrew rabua' (H7251) — foursquare; Exodus 27:1, 28:16, 30:2, Ezekiel 40:47.
Hebrew 'arba' (H702) — four; the root of the squaring.
Greek tetragonos (G5068) — four-cornered; Revelation 21:16, of the holy city.
Hebrew middah (H4060) — measure; the category the word belongs to.
Greek metreo (G3354) — to measure; the angel measures the city with a reed.
usage: “The altar shall be foursquare” — the first thing Israel met in the court.
“Foursquare it shall be being doubled” — the breastplate over the priest's heart.
“And the city lieth foursquare” — the canon ends with a measurement.

pos: n. (the front or foremost portion; Hebrew panim, Greek prora)
etymology: Old English fore, before, and part. The KJV uses it where a thing has a face — the front of the ephod, the front chamber of the temple, the bow of a ship.
biblical_def: Forepart names the side that faces outward. In the priest's vestment it fixes the rings: “And two other rings of gold thou shalt make, and shalt put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart thereof, over against the other coupling thereof, above the curious girdle of the ephod” (Exo 28:27), and the workmen did exactly so (Exo 39:20). In Solomon's temple it names the inner sanctuary as seen from the house: “And the oracle in the forepart was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof: and he overlaid it with pure gold” (1Ki 6:20). And in Luke's account of the shipwreck it names the bow: “And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves” (Act 27:41). The word is plain, but the three uses together are instructive. The forepart of the ephod is where the tribes are carried; the forepart of the temple is the cube of gold where God meets His people; the forepart of the ship is the only part that held.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forepart as the part most advanced, or first in place; the anterior part; the beginning.
webster_full: FOREPART, n. The part most advanced in place; the anterior part; as the forepart of a ship.
2. The first part in time; the beginning; as the forepart of the day.
scriptures: And two other rings of gold thou shalt make, and shalt put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart thereof, over against the other coupling thereof, above the curious girdle of the ephod.

And the oracle in the forepart was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof: and he overlaid it with pure gold; and so covered the altar which was of cedar.
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
And they made two other golden rings, and put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart of it, over against the other coupling thereof, above the curious girdle of the ephod.
corruption_summary: No significant corruption attaches to the word itself; the loss is in reading Scripture's architectural detail as filler rather than as revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's spatial detail carries doctrine. The rings of the ephod are placed toward the forepart because the breastplate bearing the twelve names must not swing loose from the priest's heart — Exodus says as much a few verses later, that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod. Where a thing is fastened tells you what it is for.

The nautical use in Acts 27 is worth holding beside the other two. Paul had been told by the angel that not a soul would be lost, and the narrative then reports, without embarrassment, that the ship broke apart. The forepart stuck fast; the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves. The promise was kept and the vessel was still destroyed. Providence is not the preservation of our arrangements; it is the keeping of God's word through the wreck of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew panim (H6440), face, front — the same word rendered face of the LORD; Greek prora (G4408), the prow of a ship.
roots_lines: Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, front, forepart; Exodus 28:27, 39:20.
Hebrew debir (H1687) — the oracle, the inner sanctuary called the forepart in 1 Kings 6:20.
Greek prora (G4408) — the prow; Acts 27:41.
Greek prumna (G4403) — the stern, the hinder part that was broken.
Hebrew 'ephod (H646) — the priestly vestment whose forepart the rings secure.
usage: “Toward the forepart thereof” — where the tribes are carried on the priest.
“The oracle in the forepart… he overlaid it with pure gold” — a cube of gold at the heart of the house.
“The forepart stuck fast” — the promise kept through the wreck.

pos: n. pl. (the two straps joining the ephod; Hebrew kathaph)
etymology: A KJV compound of shoulder, Old English sculdor, and piece, Old French piece. It renders the Hebrew word for the sides or shoulders of the priestly ephod, which bore the onyx stones.
biblical_def: The shoulderpieces are the two straps that hold the high priest's ephod together and carry the names of Israel. “It shall have the two shoulderpieces thereof joined at the two edges thereof; and so it shall be joined together” (Exo 28:7). Onto them were fastened the wreathen chains of the breastplate: “And the other two ends of the two wreathen chains thou shalt fasten in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod before it” (Exo 28:25). Bezaleel's men built them as commanded: “They made shoulderpieces for it, to couple it together: by the two edges was it coupled together” (Exo 39:4), and “the two ends of the two wreathen chains they fastened in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod, before it” (Exo 39:18). Upon these straps sat the two onyx stones engraved with the twelve tribal names, six on each. The priest could not enter the holy place without bearing Israel on his shoulders. The place of burden in Hebrew idiom is the shoulder, and the LORD put His people there — not in the priest's hand, which can set a thing down, but on his shoulders, where a load is carried until the work is finished.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the shoulder as the joint by which the arm is connected with the body, and the part on which burdens are borne; a piece is a part or fragment of a whole, or a distinct portion joined to others.
webster_full: SHOULDER, n. The joint by which the arm of a human being or the fore leg of a quadruped is connected with the body.
2. The upper joint of the fore leg cut for market.
3. In Scripture, to bear on the shoulder is to sustain, to support, to bear a burden.
PIECE, n. A fragment or part of any thing separated from the whole; a distinct part joined to others.
scriptures: Exo 28:7
It shall have the two shoulderpieces thereof joined at the two edges thereof; and so it shall be joined together.
And the other two ends of the two wreathen chains thou shalt fasten in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod before it.
Exo 39:4
They made shoulderpieces for it, to couple it together: by the two edges was it coupled together.
And the two ends of the two wreathen chains they fastened in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod, before it.
corruption_summary: Priestly mediation is reduced to ceremony, when the shoulderpieces make it a matter of weight actually carried.
corruption_paragraphs: The tabernacle assigns the tribes two positions on the priest: the shoulders and the heart. The onyx stones on the shoulderpieces bore the names for strength; the twelve stones of the breastplate bore them over the heart for love. Any account of mediation that keeps the affection and drops the burden has kept half a priest. Christ is described in Isaiah as the One upon whose shoulder the government shall be, and in Luke as the shepherd who lays the found sheep on His shoulders, rejoicing. The image is consistent and it is not decorative.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that priesthood in Scripture is never self-referential. The high priest wore no name of his own upon the ephod; he wore theirs. Ministry that turns the minister into the subject of his own office has inverted the vestment.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathaph (H3802), shoulder, side; Hebrew 'ephod (H646), the vestment; the stones borne there are shoham, onyx, engraved as a signet.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathaph (H3802) — shoulder, shoulderpiece; Exodus 28:7, 39:4.
Hebrew shoham (H7718) — onyx; the two stones set upon the shoulderpieces.
Hebrew mishbetsah (H4865) — ouches, settings of gold; Exodus 28:25.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — memorial; the stated purpose of the names on the shoulders.
Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to bear, to lift; what a shoulder does with a burden.
usage: “It shall have the two shoulderpieces thereof joined at the two edges” — the ephod is one garment because of them.
“Put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod before it” — the breastplate hangs from the shoulders.
The names on the shoulders, the names on the heart: strength and love, both borne in.

pos: n. pl. (the cast supports beneath the temple lavers; Hebrew katheph)
etymology: A KJV compound of under and setter, one that sets or places. It renders the Hebrew word for shoulder or side, here the four cast brackets at the corners of Solomon's brasen bases.
biblical_def: The undersetters appear twice in Scripture, both times in the account of Hiram's brass work for Solomon's temple. “And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition” (1Ki 7:30). The second notice adds that they were not bolted on: “And there were four undersetters to the four corners of one base: and the undersetters were of the very base itself” (1Ki 7:34). These are the brackets that carried the ten lavers, each holding forty baths of water: “Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths” (1Ki 7:38), set upon the bases of which it is written, “And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base” (1Ki 7:27). The detail that matters is the one the text insists on: the undersetters were of the very base itself. The supports were not added to the structure; they were cast with it, of one piece, so that what bore the weight and what was borne could not come apart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an undersetter as a support; a pedestal; that which is set under to sustain.
webster_full: UNDERSETTER, n. A support; a pedestal.
UNDERSET, v.t. To prop; to support; to set something under by way of support.
SET, v.t. To put or place; to fix in a standing posture.
scriptures: And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.
And there were four undersetters to the four corners of one base: and the undersetters were of the very base itself.
Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths: and every laver was four cubits: and upon every one of the ten bases one laver.
And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it.
corruption_summary: Support is imagined as something bolted on afterward, while the temple bases were cast with their supports in one piece.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one 1 Kings states outright: the undersetters were of the very base itself. Nothing that held the water of purification was an afterthought. In a house where every fitting was specified, the load-bearing parts were not fastened on at the end but poured in the same mould as the thing they carried.

The picture serves the church. Paul writes that the household of God is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone — not a support attached to an existing structure but the stone the structure is laid to. Where support is welded on late it fails late. Where it is cast in from the beginning, the base and the burden are one metal.
roots_summary: Hebrew katheph (H3802), shoulder, side, support — the same root rendered shoulderpieces in Exodus; used here of the cast brackets of the brasen bases.
roots_lines: Hebrew katheph (H3802) — shoulder, side, undersetter; 1 Kings 7:30, 7:34.
Hebrew mekonah (H4350) — base, stand; the wheeled structure the undersetters belong to.
Hebrew kiyyor (H3595) — laver; the vessel they carried.
Hebrew yatsaq (H3332) — to pour, to cast; the undersetters were molten, not fitted.
Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — brass; the metal of the whole court's furniture.
usage: “The four corners thereof had undersetters” — one at each corner, none omitted.
“The undersetters were of the very base itself” — cast in, not bolted on.
Ten lavers of forty baths apiece rested on them; the supports were the heaviest specified detail.

pos: n. pl. (the framing bars of the temple bases; Hebrew shalab)
etymology: Middle English legge, a bar or rail. The KJV uses it for the joining bars between the panels of Solomon's brasen bases, upon which the carved borders were set.
biblical_def: The ledges are the frame of the brasen bases, and Scripture describes them with a craftsman's care. “And the work of the bases was on this manner: they had borders, and the borders were between the ledges” (1Ki 7:28). What went on them is then reported: “And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work” (1Ki 7:29). The top course matched: “And in the top of the base was there a round compass of half a cubit high: and on the top of the base the ledges thereof and the borders thereof were of the same” (1Ki 7:35). And the engraving was not confined to the panels: “For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about” (1Ki 7:36). Lions, oxen, cherubims and palm trees on the frame of a washstand — the structural members of the temple court were carved as carefully as its holy furniture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ledge as a stratum or layer; a ridge; a small moulding or projecting part; a piece of timber or bar used as a frame.
webster_full: LEDGE, n. A stratum, layer or row.
2. A ridge; a prominent part; a small moulding.
3. A small piece of timber placed under the deck of a ship; a bar or frame.
4. A shelf on which things may be laid.
scriptures: And the work of the bases was on this manner: they had borders, and the borders were between the ledges:
And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work.
And in the top of the base was there a round compass of half a cubit high: and on the top of the base the ledges thereof and the borders thereof were of the same.
For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
corruption_summary: Beauty in the LORD's house is defended only where it is seen, while 1 Kings reports carving on the frame of a laver stand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's house was made beautiful in its unwatched places. The ledges are structural bars on ten wheeled stands used for washing the instruments of sacrifice, and Hiram graved cherubims, lions and palm trees upon them. Nobody worshipped the stands. They were carved anyway.

Two errors are cut off at once. The first is the utilitarian instinct that anything not directly seen may be done cheaply — refuted by the plates of the ledges. The second is the aesthetic instinct that beauty is its own justification, which the same passage refuses: every figure carved here is a figure the LORD had already authorized in the sanctuary. The lions, oxen and cherubims are not the craftsman's invention. Beauty in worship is generous, and it is still regulated.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalab (H7948), a joining bar, a rung or stay; used only of the temple bases; the panels between them are misgereth, borders.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalab (H7948) — ledge, joining bar; 1 Kings 7:28, 7:29, 7:35, 7:36.
Hebrew misgereth (H4526) — border, panel; set between the ledges.
Hebrew mekonah (H4350) — the brasen base itself.
Hebrew pathach (H6605) — to engrave, to open; the graving of cherubims and lions.
Hebrew kerub (H3742) — cherub; carved upon the frame as upon the veil.
usage: “The borders were between the ledges” — frame and panel, described like joinery.
“He graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees” — on the frame of a washstand.
The LORD's house was carved where no worshipper would look.

pos: n. pl. (cut work in stone or gold; Hebrew pittuach)
etymology: From engrave, Old English grafan, to dig or carve. The KJV uses the plural in one recurring simile: like the engravings of a signet.
biblical_def: Whenever Scripture speaks of engravings it is describing the work on the high priest's vestments, and it uses one comparison every time. “With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold” (Exo 28:11). The same for the golden plate on the mitre: “And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD” (Exo 28:36), and the record of its making repeats it word for word (Exo 39:30). The onyx stones were done accordingly: “And they wrought onyx stones inclosed in ouches of gold, graven, as signets are graven, with the names of the children of Israel” (Exo 39:6). A signet is not decoration. It is the mark by which a man's word is made binding and by which a document is proved his. Israel's names and the LORD's holiness were cut into stone and gold at signet depth — not painted, not stitched, but incised, so that what was written could not be lifted off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines engraving as the act or art of cutting figures or characters on stone, metal or wood; the work so cut.
webster_full: ENGRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting stones, metals and other hard substances, and representing thereon figures, letters or devices.
2. That which is engraved; engraved work.
ENGRAVE, v.t. To cut, as metals, stones or other hard substances, with a chisel or graver.
2. To picture or represent by incisions.
3. To imprint; to impress deeply; to infix.
scriptures: With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold.
And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD.
And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote upon it a writing, like to the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD.
Exo 39:6
And they wrought onyx stones inclosed in ouches of gold, graven, as signets are graven, with the names of the children of Israel.
corruption_summary: Identity is treated as self-declared and revisable, while Scripture cuts the names of God's people into stone at signet depth.
corruption_paragraphs: The comparison is deliberate and it is legal. A signet was pressed into wax to authenticate a document; its cut could not be argued with, and a forged seal was a capital matter. When the LORD orders the names of the tribes engraved like the engravings of a signet, He is not commissioning ornament. He is saying that the belonging of these people to Him has the standing of a sealed instrument.

This is the answer to every account of identity as a thing the self declares and may revise. The names on the onyx were not chosen by the men who bore them and could not be scratched out by them. Paul carries the figure forward when he writes that the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. What is engraved is engraved by another hand, and it holds.
roots_summary: Hebrew pittuach (H6603), engraving, carved work; from pathach (H6605), to open or cut in; chotham (H2368), a signet or seal, is the standard of comparison.
roots_lines: Hebrew pittuach (H6603) — engraving; Exodus 28:11, 28:36, 39:30.
Hebrew pathach (H6605) — to engrave, to cut in; the verb behind the noun.
Hebrew chotham (H2368) — signet, seal; the recurring point of comparison.
Hebrew charash (H2796) — craftsman, engraver in stone; Exodus 28:11.
Hebrew qodesh la-YHWH — HOLINESS TO THE LORD; the words cut into the golden plate.
usage: “Like the engravings of a signet” — the same phrase three times, never varied.
“Grave upon it… HOLINESS TO THE LORD” — cut, not written.
Names at signet depth: belonging with the standing of a sealed instrument.

pos: adj. (unmixed, unslaked; of morter that will not bind; Hebrew taphel)
etymology: From un- and temper, Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion. Morter is tempered when lime, sand and water are worked together; untempered morter is the appearance of mortar without the mixing that makes it hold.
biblical_def: Untempered occurs only in Ezekiel, and always in one indictment: the false prophets are daubing a wall. “Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter” (Eze 13:10). The LORD announces what weather will do to it: “Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it” (Eze 13:11). He then takes the work down Himself: “So will I break down the wall that ye have daubed with untempered morter, and bring it down to the ground, so that the foundation thereof shall be discovered, and it shall fall, and ye shall be consumed in the midst thereof: and ye shall know that I am the LORD” (Eze 13:14). The charge is repeated against the same class of men in the great catalogue of Jerusalem's sins: “And her prophets have daubed them with untempered morter, seeing vanity, and divining lies unto them, saying, Thus saith the Lord GOD, when the LORD hath not spoken” (Eze 22:28). Untempered morter looks exactly like morter until it rains.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines untempered as not tempered; not duly mixed for use; not softened or moderated.
webster_full: UNTEMPERED, a. Not tempered; not duly mixed or prepared.
TEMPER, v.t. To mix so that one part qualifies another; to bring to a moderate state; as, to temper mortar with sand and water.
2. To moderate; to soften; to mitigate.
MORTAR, n. A mixture of lime and sand with water, used as a cement for uniting stones and bricks.
scriptures: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it.

So will I break down the wall that ye have daubed with untempered morter, and bring it down to the ground, so that the foundation thereof shall be discovered, and it shall fall, and ye shall be consumed in the midst thereof: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
And her prophets have daubed them with untempered morter, seeing vanity, and divining lies unto them, saying, Thus saith the Lord GOD, when the LORD hath not spoken.
corruption_summary: Preaching that soothes without saying anything true is defended as pastoral warmth; Ezekiel calls it untempered morter and promises the storm.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel does not accuse these prophets of preaching heresy. He accuses them of saying Peace where there was no peace, and of covering a bad wall with something that looked like mortar. That is the exact profile of a great deal of contemporary preaching: doctrinally unobjectionable sentence by sentence, structurally load-bearing nowhere, and applied thickly over congregations whose actual condition is never named. The LORD's complaint is not that the daub was ugly. It was that it would not hold weather.

Note who takes the wall down. Not the hailstones on their own account — I will break down the wall. The judgment falls on the daubers, and it falls by exposure: the foundation thereof shall be discovered. Ministry that spares people the truth is not neutral; it builds something the storm is coming for. Ezekiel 22:28 names the aggravating offence plainly, saying, Thus saith the Lord GOD, when the LORD hath not spoken.
roots_summary: Hebrew taphel (H8602), whitewash, that which is insipid or unsalted; tuach (H2902), to daub or overlay; the pairing yields the KJV's untempered morter.
roots_lines: Hebrew taphel (H8602) — untempered, insipid, whitewash; Ezekiel 13:10, 22:28.
Hebrew tuach (H2902) — to daub, to plaster over; the action condemned.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace; the word falsely cried, Peace; and there was no peace.
Hebrew chomah (H2346) — wall; the structure the daub conceals.
Hebrew shaw' (H7723) — vanity, emptiness; what the prophets were seeing.
usage: “Saying, Peace; and there was no peace” — the indictment in six words.
“Daubed it with untempered morter” — the look of a binding without the binding.
“There shall be an overflowing shower” — the test every ministry eventually meets.
